COLOR FROM GLASS
MethodResultsGallery
Image alignment · project study

Three exposures.
One color image.

A century-old color photograph starts as three monochrome plates. By finding where the green and red exposures belong relative to blue, we can bring the scene back together.

18 supplied plates · 13 small JPEGs · 5 large scans

01 / The approach

Split, compare, refine.

Each file stacks the blue, green, and red exposures vertically. I split it into equal thirds and use blue as the fixed reference. A candidate shift moves green or red horizontally and vertically; the best score wins. Offsets below are (x, y) pixels applied to the moving channel, with positive x right and positive y down.

01 · SINGLE SCALE

Search the small plates

For the 13 small JPEGs, test every integer shift within ±15 pixels. The score uses a consistent interior region, so a shift cannot win merely by reducing overlap.

02 · PYRAMID

Start small, then sharpen

A five-tap blur precedes each 2× downsample. Search ±15 at the coarsest level, double the estimate on the next level, and refine within ±2 pixels until full resolution.

03 · FINISH

Trim the fringes

Shift both channels, keep their common valid overlap, then detect black, white, and saturated scan borders independently on each side. The delivered images use NCC.

Two ways to score a match. NCC is uncentered normalized cross-correlation; maximizing it rewards a similar pattern even when channel brightness differs. L2 minimizes root mean squared pixel difference. Both were evaluated with the same search and interior support.
02 / See the shift

From colored edges to a coherent scene.

These composites use identical source plates. The left images stack the channels with zero offset; the right images apply the NCC pyramid offsets before final border trimming.

04 / Where it struggles

Matching brightness is not always matching structure.

Most offsets agree closely across metrics. A few exposed the limits of intensity matching: the L2 pyramid lands on a very different red shift for the ornate wall in 01269v.jpg and the dark interior in 01725u.jpg. The coarse search can lock onto a repeated or similarly bright region; later ±2 refinements cannot escape it. In 00804v.jpg, NCC itself chooses a red x shift of −30 instead of the single-scale and L2 value of −4, leaving visible color separation. Some colored fringes also persist in 00056v.jpg because the three photographic exposures differ in tone and detail; pure translation cannot make every edge identical.

The final crop removes invalid rolled pixels and many scan borders; it does not repair a wrong match. An edge-based score or a check against the single-scale estimate would be useful next experiments.

The attached data bundle supplied all 18 source plates. No separate Prokudin-Gorskii downloads were provided, so this gallery uses selected examples from that bundle rather than claiming additional acquisitions.

Built from the supplied part_two.py, source plates, and output archive. The original implementation also includes common-overlap cropping, a consistent comparison window, Gaussian-style pyramid smoothing, and automatic four-side border detection.
